Top Overnight News

Deadly Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital’s main airport over the weekend raised the risk of a wider war that may draw in the US. More missiles and drones were intercepted overnight. BBG

The United States' response to Iran's seven conditions in a proposal to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was "insufficient", Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, was quoted by state media on Sunday as saying. RTRS

Oil swung after US President Donald Trump said Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to an “energy ceasefire,” while in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest strikes since the Iran war began. BBG

Ukraine will continue to respond with long-range strikes against Russia unless Moscow agrees to an energy ceasefire that still hasn’t happened, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday. BBG

Saudi Arabia is looking at ways to expand its oil pipeline capacity to destinations outside the Persian Gulf to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years, said Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman. BBG

US Senators reportedly demanded that President Trump reverse the Russian fuel imports deal, while Republican Senator Tillis warned that Trump’s Russian diesel deal may be illegal and put American lives at risk. Newsquawk

The EU will cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 a year starting as soon as Dec. 1, with the limit rising 6% annually from the second year, according to a document seen by Bloomberg. The effect is likely to be more restrictive for Chinese automakers than tariffs, BI said. BBG

China passenger vehicle sales tumbled 28% Y/Y in Sept, the largest so far this year and a sign that the domestic market remains under pressure. Nikkei

Nvidia is in talks to acquire or deepen its investment in US start-up Reflection AI, a developer of open-weight models that President Donald Trump’s administration hopes will rival cheap Chinese alternatives, people with direct knowledge of the matter said. FT

AZMN is in talks to acquire artificial-intelligence startup Decart in a deal that could be valued at around $7 billion. San Francisco-based Decart’s software makes it easier for developers to switch between different AI chips, a capability that is becoming increasingly important as companies race to secure more computing power. WSJ

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said on Monday that capital will be the biggest constraint facing the company as AI development continues. RTRS

Nato members should prepare a robust response for a possible deadly Russian “hybrid” attack, Poland’s foreign minister has said, as concern grows about Moscow’s escalating sabotage campaign on European soil. FT

France’s bonds resumed declines. Investors are losing faith in its ability to get a grip on its debt and growing increasingly concerned about the risk of contagion.

Germany’s fragile government was plunged deeper into turmoil on Monday after the labor minister and co-chair of the junior coalition partner abruptly resigned from both her posts. BBG

Bond markets are starting to do some of the lifting for central banks around the world by pushing up borrowing costs themselves, potentially reducing the number of benchmark interest-rate hikes needed to get inflation under control. BBG

India’s consumer prices rose 5.54% Y/Y in September, vs est. +5.58%, the highest in almost two years and backing RBI tightening. BBG

Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on stabilization. BBG

Goldman raised its Dec 2026 Brent forecast to $90/bbl from $85 and still sees Brent averaging $80 in 2027; in an upside scenario where Gulf output stays 5mb/d below February levels, Brent could average around $125 in 2027. GIR

JPM's Feroli sees September headline CPI at +0.55% M/M (3.6% Y/Y) and core at +0.18% (2.4% Y/Y), enough to keep the bond market from re-pricing an October hike. JPM

tweets.text:
US seasonal hiring is off to a weak start:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 90,787 workers in September, the weakest September total since 2011.

This marks a -23% decline from the 117,313 recorded in September 2025.

Retail led all industries last month, with 65,150 announced hires, followed by Aerospace and Defense at 5,300.

However, announced seasonal hiring is muted so far this year, with a combined 62,000 seasonal hires, compared with 100,800 announced by seasonal employers last September.

Year-to-date, US hiring plans have totaled 210,612 workers, the 2nd-lowest total for the first 9 months of the year in at least 10 years.

Retail leads all sectors with 66,557 announcements so far in 2026, followed by Technology, at 22,361, and Aerospace and Defense, at 21,841.

Hiring demand remains muted.

A month ago the bond market was bracing for a wave of rate hikes. That bet is unwinding fast.

Since mid-September, 12-month hike pricing has shrunk across almost every major economy. Australia down 47 basis points, the euro zone down 43, Korea down 22, the US down 19. Only China nudged higher.

The bond selloff did the tightening for the central banks, so the central banks step back.

Fewer hikes ahead takes pressure off long yields, and that is a tailwind for risk assets.

🌎🚨 Bond markets are starting to do central banks' job for them as investors have priced out nearly 180 basis points of expected rate hikes across eight major economies.

📉 Rising bond yields are tightening financial conditions without central banks having to intervene. Households face higher borrowing costs, companies have to finance their investments at less favorable rates, and governments are gradually seeing their refinancing costs increase. All of this weighs on economic activity and could therefore reduce the need for central banks to raise policy rates further. The cumulative rate hikes expected over the next 12 months across eight economies have fallen from 717 to 539 basis points since September.

⚠️ However, not all increases in long-term yields are created equal. If yields are rising because the economy is strong or investors expect persistent inflation, that's one thing, but if they're rising because markets are demanding higher risk premiums to finance government deficits, that's a different story. Right now, we're dealing with a combination of both. Between massive US deficits, concerns over France's public finances, enormous AI-related financing needs and the energy shock triggered by the conflict with Iran, the pressure on long-term yields goes well beyond monetary policy. I believe the risk is that central banks stop raising rates, or even start cutting them, without financial conditions actually improving.

➡️ There is another thing that I believe is fundamental. If long-term yields keep climbing despite policy rates stabilizing, we could see renewed discussions around slowing QT, Operation Twist-style interventions, or outright bond purchases. None of this is inevitable or necessarily desirable as intervening to suppress yields while inflation remains elevated could undermine monetary credibility and fuel even higher risk premiums.

For years, markets were mainly worried about central banks tightening financial conditions too aggressively, but now the risk is that they may no longer be able to ease financial conditions sufficiently, even when they want to.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/iV58Caf7pk

I've had a few DMs asking why I've been posting walls of text lately instead of my usual macro charts.

Fair question… it's not like me. I'm a visual thinker and learner. My usual macro updates are really just a huge string of charts that, when pieced together, tell the whole story.

Right now I'm rebuilding my entire macro database from scratch. Anyone who knows how many charts I typically work with knows that's a fairly daunting task.

The unexpected benefit is that it forces me to revisit everything I've ever built with a fresh pair of eyes. Charts, indicators, and business cycle frameworks I've used for years are being questioned, rebuilt, and improved.

The charts are coming back, and they'll be better than ever. Expect all the usual macro chart mayhem to return next month…

The supply overhang that crushed alts has dissipated and is, for the first time in the asset class's history, manageable.

Payouts to holders minus new supply, as a share of market value:
2021-22: -17% a year
2026: -2.9%

Tokens paying holders more than they dilute them: 4% then, 17% now.

Part of this is capital discipline. Better unlock management, maturing protocols, and revenue-funded buybacks. Tokens are starting to take on equity-like properties.

The other part is demand. It's showing up. Tokenisation first, and eventually AI agentic commerce.

Less drag, more demand. Structurally, crypto has never been in better shape.

@RealVision
